title: GPU Tenant Sandboxing: Privacy Shield, Egress Partitioning, and Sandbox Patterns
author: Priya Nair
content:
Overview:

This document describes a repeatable, platform-native approach for creating GPU inference sandboxes for tenants that combine strong privacy guarantees (the Privacy Shield pattern), network egress partitioning, and developer-friendly IaC modules. The guidance is targeted at platform engineers who build self-serve tenant sandboxes (ephemeral or long-lived) used for model evaluation, partner integrations, and regulated PoCs.

Goals:
- Provide an operational pattern that prevents accidental egress of tenant data to external endpoints without explicit approval.
- Offer templates (Terraform + CI gating) so product teams can request sandboxes with predictable security posture.
- Enable cost control and capacity isolation for GPU-backed sandboxes while preserving developer ergonomics.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood-managed GPU pools in public clouds (AWS/GCP) and hybrid on-prem nodes that are attached to the same control plane.
- Assumes tenants run inference workloads through Redwood serving runtime and use the platform's token-to-tenant routing.
- Not a replacement for formal legal/compliance reviews; it simplifies engineering controls required by internal audits.

Key Concepts and Patterns:

1) Privacy Shield (network-first tenant isolation)
- Definition: An enforced network and KMS boundary around a tenant sandbox that prevents outbound connections except through an allowlist of approved proxies or egress gateways.
- Components:
  - VPC namespace with host route hygiene and no default internet gateway.
  - Egress Gateways (proxy clusters) running inside a restricted account/namespace; all outbound flow must pass through them.
  - Egress ACLs enforced at both cloud-network (NACL/SG) and service (proxy policy) layers.
  - Tenant-scoped encryption keys (KMS) where possible; sandbox secrets are encrypted under tenant keys and separated in secret stores.

2) Egress Partitioning and Rate Limiting
- Rationale: Sandboxes are often used to call external APIs during model evaluation. Partitioning ensures a noisy tenant cannot consume the shared proxy or blow budget.
- Patterns:
  - Logical buckets: create per-tenant or per-project egress buckets which map to rate-limiter tokens in the proxy.
  - Token quota enforcement: tie per-tenant API keys to rate and cost budgets; enforce server-side quotas with 429+retry-after semantics.
  - Billing tags: annotate proxy egress with tenant IDs for chargeback and alerting.

3) Ephemeral Credentials and Short-lived Workloads
- Use short-lived IAM tokens for any sandbox service accounts; refresh period <= 1 hour.
- Limit long-running operator access: a separate control-plane agent with elevated privileges handles onboarding and rotation.

4) IaC Modules and Self-Serve API
- Provide a small set of Terraform modules for sandbox creation: network (vpc-sandbox), compute (gpu-pool-binding), egress (egress-gateway-binding), and secrets (tenant-kms-binding).
- Expose a single YAML spec that product teams can submit via the self-service portal or a PR. Minimal required fields: tenant_id, sandbox_tier, estimated_gpu_hours, egress_allowlist.

Sandbox Onboarding Playbook (Operator and Self-Serve flows):

Operator-assisted (for regulated tenants):
1. Receive request with YAML spec and compliance checklist.
2. Provision VPC namespace via terraform module vpc-sandbox; do not attach an Internet Gateway.
3. Bind GPU pool using nft/gpu-pool-binding module with explicit tenant tag.
4. Deploy egress-gateway in restricted account and link proxy policy for tenant.
5. Create tenant KMS key alias and grant decrypt to runtime-role only.
6. Run smoke tests: DNS, proxy allowlist, key decrypt, runtime checklist.
7. Hand off to tenant with sandbox-runbook and pre-populated credentials.

Self-serve (developer-friendly):
1. Developer opens the self-serve portal and submits minimal spec.
2. Automated CI triggers: terraform plan -> policy checks (OPA/Gatekeeper) -> terraform apply in sandbox account.
3. Post-apply steps: create short-lived credentials via token service, create cost alert and cost center tag.
4. Send onboarding email with CLI snippets and example prompts.

Terraform module configuration matrix (reference):

| Module | Required inputs | Outputs | Notes |
|--------|-----------------|---------|-------|
| vpc-sandbox | tenant_id, cidr_block, region | vpc_id, private_subnet_ids | No IGW, nat disabled by default |
| gpu-pool-binding | tenant_id, instance_profile, max_gpus | pool_attachment_id | Attach to pre-provisioned hetero-pool |
| egress-gateway-binding | tenant_id, allowlist_domains, quota_per_minute | proxy_endpoint, quota_token | Integrates with envoy-based rate limiter |
| tenant-kms-binding | tenant_id, rotation_days | kms_alias, key_arn | Grants decrypt to runtime-role only |

Policy and CI gating checklist (examples):
- Terraform plan must show no IGW/route to 0.0.0.0/0 in public subnets.
- OPA rule: "sandbox-must-not-have-public-ssh": deny if any security group permits 0.0.0.0/0:22.
- Cost estimate threshold: block apply if projected monthly GPU spend > $5k without approval.
- Secret leakage scan: deny if terraform state contains plaintext keys.

Runtime integration specifics:
- Serving runtime must:
  - Label requests with tenant_id and sandbox=true.
  - Persist KV cache to tenant-scoped storage buckets with server-side encryption and lifecycle TTL (default 7d).
  - Emit egress metrics: egress_bytes, egress_requests, egress_rate_429, labeled by tenant_id and proxy_token.

Operational SLOs and alerts:
- Sandbox control-plane apply success rate >= 98% (daily). Alert if < 95% for 30m.
- Egress gateway 95th p99 latency <= 350ms for allowed domains; alert on sustained > 1s.
- Quota exhaustion: send CRITICAL alert and notify tenant owner via 15-min page if automatic quota top-up not configured.

Incident playbook (egress bypass detected):
1. Pager duty: on-call infra lead.
2. Identify offending sandbox via egress telemetry and tags.
3. Isolate: remove proxy token, revoke sandbox service role, and block egress at cloud firewall.
4. Snapshot terraform state and audit logs.
5. Rehydrate environment into a quarantine account for forensics.
6. Postmortem and update OPA/Gatekeeper policies.

Example CLI snippets for tenants (delivered in onboarding email):
- Acquire ephemeral token:
  curl -X POST https://token.redwood.internal/v1/acquire -d '{"tenant":"T-123","ttl":3600}'

- Run a sandboxed job with proxy endpoint:
  export PROXY_ENDPOINT=https://proxy.redwood.internal/T-123
  ENV_PROXY=$PROXY_ENDPOINT ./run-inference.sh --model small-quantized

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Platform infra: maintain terraform modules, OPA policies, CI pipelines, and template gallery.
- GPU fleet team: enforce pool tagging, capacity reservations, and billing exports.
- Security: approve sensitive tenant allowlist requests and review KMS bindings.
- Customer Success / Sales: provide compliance packages and escalation path for partners.

Rollout plan (90 days):
- Week 1-2: ship vpc-sandbox and egress-gateway-binding modules + CI policy checks.
- Week 3-5: pilot with two internal product teams (non-sensitive).
- Week 6-10: iterate on cost-control telemetry and quota UX.
- Week 11-13: enable operator-assisted workflow for regulated customers and document audit steps.

References and related artifacts:
- Examples: /repo/infra/terraform/modules/vpc-sandbox/README.md
- OPA policy pack: /repo/infra/policies/sandbox-opa.rego
- Egress gateway design doc: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-gateway-design

Appendix: common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Developers adding public egress in app layer. Mitigation: CI scanning and post-deploy egress telemetry alerts.
- Pitfall: Unbounded egress quotas for third-party model evaluation. Mitigation: default 100 req/min token and automated approval for higher budgets.

If you plan to pilot this pattern, open an RFC in #infra-sandbox or submit a ticket to the platform backlog with the tenant_id, estimated GPU-hours, and compliance tier.
